key_definitions.opportunity_cost: The next best alternative foregone when making a choice.
key_definitions.PPC: Shows maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with given resources at full employment.
key_definitions.factors_of_production: Land (natural resources), Labour (human effort), Capital (man-made resources), Enterprise (risk-taking).

mcq_traps: Do not confuse 'movement along PPC' (efficient production) with 'shift of PPC' (change in productive capacity).
Opportunity cost is always the NEXT BEST alternative, not just any alternative lost.
Capital goods are man-made, not money or financial assets.

key_definitions.market_failure: When the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently.
key_definitions.externality: A cost or benefit affecting a third party not involved in the transaction.
key_definitions.public_good: Non-excludable and non-rival (e.g. street lighting, national defence).
key_definitions.merit_good: A good under-consumed in a free market (e.g. education, healthcare).
key_definitions.demerit_good: A good over-consumed in a free market (e.g. cigarettes, alcohol).

mcq_traps: Public goods: BOTH non-excludable AND non-rival must be true.
Merit goods are NOT the same as public goods — merit goods can be provided privately.
Negative externality → social cost > private cost (market over-produces).
Positive externality → social benefit > private benefit (market under-produces).

key_definitions.demand: The willingness and ability to buy a product at a given price.
key_definitions.law_of_demand: As price rises, quantity demanded falls (ceteris paribus).
key_definitions.PED: Price Elasticity of Demand = % change in QD / % change in Price.

mcq_traps: MOVEMENT along demand curve = change in PRICE only.
SHIFT of demand curve = change in any other determinant (income, tastes, etc.).
If PED > 1 → elastic: lower price increases total revenue.
If PED < 1 → inelastic: higher price increases total revenue.
Giffen good: inferior good where demand RISES as price RISES (very rare exception).

key_definitions.supply: The willingness and ability of producers to sell at a given price.
key_definitions.law_of_supply: As price rises, quantity supplied rises (ceteris paribus).
key_definitions.PES: Price Elasticity of Supply = % change in QS / % change in Price.
key_definitions.subsidy: A payment from government to producers to lower costs and increase supply.
key_definitions.indirect_tax: A tax on goods/services that shifts supply curve left.

mcq_traps: A subsidy shifts supply RIGHT (increases) — it reduces costs for producers.
An indirect tax shifts supply LEFT (decreases) — it increases costs for producers.
PES is inelastic if: few spare resources, production takes a long time, perishable goods.
Joint supply: producing more of one good automatically produces more of another (e.g. beef and leather).
If price is ABOVE equilibrium → excess supply → price falls.
If price is BELOW equilibrium → excess demand → price rises.
In a free market, price acts as both signal AND incentive simultaneously.

key_definitions.GDP: Total value of goods and services produced within a country in one year.
key_definitions.inflation: A sustained rise in the general price level.
key_definitions.unemployment: People who are willing and able to work but cannot find a job.
key_definitions.aggregate_demand: Total spending in an economy: C + I + G + (X - M).
key_definitions.fiscal_policy: Government use of taxation and spending to influence the economy.
key_definitions.monetary_policy: Central bank control of interest rates and money supply.

mcq_traps: Real GDP adjusts for inflation; nominal GDP does not.
Cyclical unemployment rises in recession; structural unemployment is due to change in industry.
Current account deficit means imports > exports (value of goods and services).
Expansionary fiscal policy = increase spending OR cut taxes.

key_definitions.comparative_advantage: Produce the good with the LOWEST opportunity cost.
key_definitions.quota: A physical limit on the quantity of imports.
key_definitions.exchange_rate: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another.

mcq_traps: Comparative advantage is about OPPORTUNITY COST, not absolute output.
A fall in exchange rate → exports cheaper → exports rise; imports dearer → imports fall.
Tariff raises government revenue; quota does NOT.
Appreciation of currency → exports more expensive → current account likely worsens.

key_definitions.functions_of_money: Medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account, standard of deferred payment.
key_definitions.interest_rate: The cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving.

mcq_traps: Higher interest rates → less borrowing → less spending → inflation may fall.
Central bank controls monetary policy; government controls fiscal policy.
Money must satisfy ALL four functions — barter only satisfies exchange.

key_definitions.maximum_price: Set BELOW equilibrium to keep goods affordable → causes shortage.
key_definitions.minimum_price: Set ABOVE equilibrium to protect producers/workers → causes surplus.
key_definitions.minimum_wage: A minimum price for labour — set above equilibrium → unemployment may rise.

mcq_traps: Maximum price causes SHORTAGE (excess demand).
Minimum price causes SURPLUS (excess supply).
Minimum wage only matters if set ABOVE the market wage rate.
Subsidies help producers; maximum prices help consumers.

exam_tips: Read every option carefully — 'quantity demanded' vs 'demand' are different (movement vs shift).
Eliminate obviously wrong options first, then use economic theory to choose between remaining options.
Look for words like 'ceteris paribus' — it means all other things are held equal.
Diagrams described in MCQs: always trace through the effect step by step.
For elasticity MCQs: remember PED inelastic goods (necessities) vs elastic goods (luxuries).
For macroeconomics MCQs: AD = C + I + G + (X - M) is your key formula.
Opportunity cost: always identify WHAT is given up, not just that something IS given up.
Cambridge 2281 distractors often confuse cause and effect — trace the chain of logic carefully.
YED negative = inferior good; YED positive = normal good; YED > 1 = luxury good.
Market failure means FREE MARKET fails — not that all markets fail.

Effects of indirect taxes and subsidies
